claim: OCT4 is a pluripotency-associated pioneer factor that binds chromatin to shape accessibility, transcription factor co-binding, and regulatory element function in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: Here, we discover that the pluripotency-associated pioneer factor OCT4 binds chromatin to shape accessibility, transcription factor co-binding, and regulatory element function in mouse embryonic stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Chromatin accessibility at OCT4-bound sites requires the chromatin remodeller BRG1.
source: Chromatin accessibility at OCT4-bound sites requires the chromatin remodeller BRG1, which is recruited to these sites by OCT4 to support additional transcription factor binding and expression of the pluripotency-associated transcriptome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: BRG1 is recruited to OCT4-bound sites by OCT4.
source: Chromatin accessibility at OCT4-bound sites requires the chromatin remodeller BRG1, which is recruited to these sites by OCT4 to support additional transcription factor binding and expression of the pluripotency-associated transcriptome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 4 showing loss of BRG1 binding upon OCT4 depletion.

claim: BRG1 supports additional transcription factor binding at OCT4-bound sites.
source: Chromatin accessibility at OCT4-bound sites requires the chromatin remodeller BRG1, which is recruited to these sites by OCT4 to support additional transcription factor binding and expression of the pluripotency-associated transcriptome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 5 showing reduced SOX2 and NANOG binding upon BRG1 depletion.

claim: The requirement for BRG1 in shaping OCT4 binding reflects how these target sites are used during cellular reprogramming and early mouse development.
source: Furthermore, the requirement for BRG1 in shaping OCT4 binding reflects how these target sites are used during cellular reprogramming and early mouse development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by analysis of reprogramming and developmental data in Figure 6.

claim: Transcription factors in prokaryotes recognize extended DNA sequences with high specificity and affinity.
source: In prokaryotes, transcription factors tend to function as self-contained units that recognize extended DNA sequences with high specificity and affinity (Wunderlich and Mirny, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wunderlich and Mirny, 2009.

claim: Transcription factors in higher eukaryotes recognize shorter DNA sequences than prokaryotic transcription factors.
source: In contrast, transcription factors in higher eukaryotes recognize shorter DNA sequences and often interface with other DNA-binding transcription factors in a combinatorial manner to achieve affinity and specificity (Wunderlich and Mirny, 2009; Villar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wunderlich and Mirny, 2009 and Villar et al., 2014.

claim: Eukaryotic transcription factors often interface with other DNA-binding transcription factors in a combinatorial manner to achieve affinity and specificity.
source: In contrast, transcription factors in higher eukaryotes recognize shorter DNA sequences and often interface with other DNA-binding transcription factors in a combinatorial manner to achieve affinity and specificity (Wunderlich and Mirny, 2009; Villar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wunderlich and Mirny, 2009 and Villar et al., 2014.

claim: Eukaryotic DNA is wrapped around histones to form nucleosomes and chromatin.
source: In addition to the widespread requirement for combinatorial DNA binding, eukaryotic transcription factors are also confronted with the added complexity that eukaryotic DNA is wrapped around histones to form nucleosomes and chromatin (Kornberg and Lorch, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kornberg and Lorch, 1999 and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: The association of DNA with nucleosomes can compete with DNA-binding transcription factors, limiting their ability to engage with the genome.
source: The association of DNA with nucleosomes can therefore compete with DNA-binding transcription factors, limiting their ability to engage with the genome (Spitz and Furlong, 2012; Voss and Hager, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spitz and Furlong, 2012 and Voss and Hager, 2014.

claim: In many cases transcription factor binding appears to require pre-existing chromatin accessibility.
source: Indeed, in many cases transcription factor binding appears to require pre-existing chromatin accessibility (Guertin and Lis, 2010; Biddie et al., 2011; John et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guertin and Lis, 2010; Biddie et al., 2011; and John et al., 2011.

claim: FoxA1 binds to and de-compacts nucleosomal DNA in vitro.
source: This is exemplified by the forkhead box A1 (FoxA1) transcription factor, which binds to and de-compacts nucleosomal DNA in vitro (Cirillo et al., 2002) and in vivo (Holmqvist et al., 2005; Lupien et al., 2008; Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cirillo et al., 2002.

claim: FoxA1 binds to and de-compacts nucleosomal DNA in vivo.
source: This is exemplified by the forkhead box A1 (FoxA1) transcription factor, which binds to and de-compacts nucleosomal DNA in vitro (Cirillo et al., 2002) and in vivo (Holmqvist et al., 2005; Lupien et al., 2008; Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holmqvist et al., 2005; Lupien et al., 2008; and Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016.

claim: Pioneer transcription factors play a primary role in recognizing and shaping how new gene regulatory elements are established in previously inaccessible chromatin.
source: Based on this type of activity, factors like FoxA1 have been called 'pioneer' transcription factors as they appear to play a primary role in recognizing and shaping how new gene regulatory elements are established in previously inaccessible chromatin (Magnani et al., 2011; Zaret and Carroll, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Magnani et al., 2011 and Zaret and Carroll, 2011.

claim: Pioneer transcription factors create accessible chromatin once bound to their target sites.
source: Once bound to their target sites, pioneer transcription factors appear to create accessible chromatin (Raposo et al., 2015; Schulz et al., 2015) that supports the recruitment of non-pioneer transcription factors and the formation of functional gene regulatory elements (Theodorou et al., 2013; Wapinski et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014; Schulz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raposo et al., 2015 and Schulz et al., 2015.

claim: Pioneer transcription factors support the recruitment of non-pioneer transcription factors and the formation of functional gene regulatory elements.
source: Once bound to their target sites, pioneer transcription factors appear to create accessible chromatin (Raposo et al., 2015; Schulz et al., 2015) that supports the recruitment of non-pioneer transcription factors and the formation of functional gene regulatory elements (Theodorou et al., 2013; Wapinski et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014; Schulz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Theodorou et al., 2013; Wapinski et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014; and Schulz et al., 2015.

claim: FoxA1 and FoxO1 structurally resemble histone H1.
source: For example, FoxA1 and FoxO1 structurally resemble histone H1, which has been proposed to lead to displacement of H1 and destabilisation of neighbouring nucleosomes (Cirillo et al., 2002; Hatta and Cirillo, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cirillo et al., 2002 and Hatta and Cirillo, 2007.

claim: ATP-dependent chromatin remodellers may be required to assist pioneer transcription factors in establishing accessible chromatin.
source: Alternatively, it has been proposed that ATP-dependent chromatin remodellers may be required to assist pioneer transcription factors in establishing accessible chromatin (Hu et al., 2011; Marathe et al., 2013; Ceballos-Chávez et al., 2015; Swinstead et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2011; Marathe et al., 2013; Ceballos-Chávez et al., 2015; and Swinstead et al., 2016.

claim: The Yamanaka transcription factors (OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC) can reprogram somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: One paradigm that has been used to study pioneer transcription factor function is the cellular reprogramming of somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) by the Yamanaka transcription factors (OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC) (Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006.

claim: OCT4, SOX2, and KLF4 are proposed to act as pioneers during cellular reprogramming.
source: With the exception of c-MYC, these transcription factors are proposed to act as pioneers during cellular reprogramming and can bind their targets sites even when they are occupied by nucleosomes (Soufi et al., 2012, 2015; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soufi et al., 2012, 2015 and Chen et al., 2016.

claim: OCT4, SOX2, and KLF4 can bind their target sites even when they are occupied by nucleosomes.
source: With the exception of c-MYC, these transcription factors are proposed to act as pioneers during cellular reprogramming and can bind their targets sites even when they are occupied by nucleosomes (Soufi et al., 2012, 2015; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soufi et al., 2012, 2015 and Chen et al., 2016.

claim: 15,920 high-confidence OCT4 binding sites were identified in mouse ESCs that were lost following doxycycline treatment.
source: Analysis of our OCT4 ChIP-seq identified 15,920 high-confidence OCT4 binding sites that were lost following doxycycline treatment (Figure 1C) and were highly enriched for known OCT4 binding motifs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1C and motif analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: 75% of OCT4 binding events correspond to distal regulatory elements with high H3K4me1/low H3K4me3 signature.
source: The majority of these binding events (75%) correlated with a histone modification signature usually associated with distal regulatory elements (high H3K4me1/low H3K4me3), while only a small subset (6.8%) corresponded to sites with a promoter associated histone modification signature (high H3K4me3/low H3K4me1) (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by histone modification analysis shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: 6.8% of OCT4 binding events correspond to promoters with high H3K4me3/low H3K4me1 signature.
source: The majority of these binding events (75%) correlated with a histone modification signature usually associated with distal regulatory elements (high H3K4me1/low H3K4me3), while only a small subset (6.8%) corresponded to sites with a promoter associated histone modification signature (high H3K4me3/low H3K4me1) (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by histone modification analysis shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: OCT4 binds extensively to distal as opposed to promoter proximal regulatory regions in the genome.
source: These observations are consistent with previous reports indicating that OCT4 binds extensively to distal as opposed to promoter proximal regulatory regions in the genome (Chen et al., 2008; Göke et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2008 and Göke et al., 2011, and by the data in Figure 1D.

claim: 72% of OCT4 targets showed significant reductions in chromatin accessibility following OCT4 depletion.
source: Although OCT4-bound sites were highly accessible in wild type cells, when we examined ATAC-seq signal in the OCT4-depleted ESCs, 72% of OCT4 targets showed significant reductions in chromatin accessibility (Figure 1E,F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and increases in nucleosome occupancy (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 1E,F,G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and nucleosome occupancy data in Figure 1H.

claim: OCT4-bound sites showed increases in nucleosome occupancy following OCT4 depletion.
source: Although OCT4-bound sites were highly accessible in wild type cells, when we examined ATAC-seq signal in the OCT4-depleted ESCs, 72% of OCT4 targets showed significant reductions in chromatin accessibility (Figure 1E,F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and increases in nucleosome occupancy (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by nucleosome occupancy data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: OCT4-bound distal regulatory elements were most significantly affected by loss of chromatin accessibility, while OCT4-bound promoters experienced few significant reductions in accessibility.
source: Importantly, OCT4-bound distal regulatory elements appeared to be most significantly affected, while OCT4-bound promoters experienced few significant reductions in accessibility (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1I comparing distal regulatory elements and promoters.

claim: Many OCT4-bound regulatory elements were completely inaccessible in OCT4-depleted ESCs.
source: Consistent with a pioneering-like role for OCT4 in shaping chromatin structure, many OCT4-bound regulatory elements were completely inaccessible in the OCT4-depleted ESCs (Figure 1F,J) and lacked any detectable chromatin accessibility in cells and tissues lacking OCT4 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 1F,J and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: OCT4-bound regulatory elements lacked detectable chromatin accessibility in cells and tissues lacking OCT4 expression.
source: Consistent with a pioneering-like role for OCT4 in shaping chromatin structure, many OCT4-bound regulatory elements were completely inaccessible in the OCT4-depleted ESCs (Figure 1F,J) and lacked any detectable chromatin accessibility in cells and tissues lacking OCT4 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by DNase-seq data from multiple cell lines and tissues shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: OCT4 binding sites that displayed reduced accessibility following OCT4 removal were often in close proximity with genes implicated in the pluripotency regulatory network.
source: Importantly, OCT4 binding sites that displayed reduced accessibility following OCT4 removal were often in close proximity with genes implicated in the pluripotency regulatory network (Figure 1K), suggesting that these OCT4 binding events may be implicated with the maintenance of pluripotency-associated gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Major reductions in SOX2 and NANOG binding were observed at OCT4 target sites that experienced the largest reductions in chromatin accessibility.
source: Interestingly, we observed major reductions in SOX2 and NANOG binding at the OCT4 target sites that experienced the largest reductions in chromatin accessibility (Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data for SOX2 and NANOG shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The reductions in SOX2 and NANOG binding correlated extremely well with the reductions in chromatin accessibility at OCT4-bound sites.
source: Importantly, the reductions in SOX2 and NANOG binding correlated extremely well with the reductions in chromatin accessibility at OCT4-bound sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: OCT4-bound sites that retained chromatin accessibility following OCT4 depletion retained SOX2 or NANOG occupancy.
source: Conversely, the smaller subset of OCT4-bound sites that retained chromatin accessibility following OCT4 depletion retained SOX2 or NANOG occupancy (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Loss of OCT4-dependent chromatin accessibility and transcription factor binding was broadly associated with the down-regulation of nearby genes.
source: To understand whether this loss of combinatorial transcription factor binding was relevant to gene regulation, we carried out nuclear RNA-seq in wild type and OCT4-depleted cells. Loss of OCT4-dependent chromatin accessibility and transcription factor binding was broadly associated with the down-regulation of nearby genes (Figure 2C–E), such as the pluripotency-associated Utf1 gene (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: 82% of genes with reduced expression near OCT4-bound distal sites showed coincident reductions in chromatin accessibility.
source: When we examined this relationship across the genome, reductions in the expression of genes near OCT4-bound distal sites was highly coincident (82%) with reductions in chromatin accessibility (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Genes that were down-regulated in OCT4-depleted ESCs tended to be significantly closer to OCT4 binding sites that displayed reduced chromatin accessibility (median distance 16.2 kb) than OCT4 binding sites that retained chromatin accessibility (median distance 125.4 kb).
source: Nevertheless, genes that were down-regulated in OCT4-depleted ESCs (n = 1430; OCT4-dependent gene expression) tended to be significantly closer to OCT4 binding sites that displayed reduced chromatin accessibility (median distance 16.2 kb) than OCT4 binding sites that retained chromatin accessibility in the absence of OCT4 (median distance 125.4 kb) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Genes down-regulated after loss of OCT4 are enriched for the pluripotency transcriptional network.
source: These sites were also characterized by reductions in SOX2 and NANOG binding (Figure 2A,B) and their associated genes were enriched for the pluripotency-associated transcriptional network (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Of nine individual chromatin remodelling complexes examined, only BRG1 showed an appreciable correlation between occupancy and the reliance on OCT4 for chromatin accessibility.
source: Remarkably, of the nine individual chromatin remodelling complexes examined, only BRG1 (SMARCA4), a catalytic ATPase subunit of the vertebrate SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex (also referred to as BRG1-associated factor (BAF) remodelling complexes), showed an appreciable correlation between occupancy and the reliance on OCT4 for chromatin accessibility (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A comparing nine chromatin remodellers.

claim: BRG1 was significantly enriched at regulatory elements that relied on OCT4 for chromatin accessibility.
source: Indeed, BRG1 was significantly enriched at regulatory elements that relied on OCT4 for chromatin accessibility (OCT4-dependent ATAC peaks) and regulatory elements bound by OCT4 (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: OCT4 and BRG1 occupancy was highly correlated throughout the mouse ESC genome.
source: Furthermore, OCT4 and BRG1 occupancy was highly correlated throughout the mouse ESC genome (Figure 3E and Ho et al. (2009), Kidder et al. (2009), de Dieuleveult et al., 2016), supporting the possibility that there may be a functional link between OCT4 binding, BRG1, and chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is supported by genome-wide correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E and citations to Ho et al. (2009), Kidder et al. (2009), and de Dieuleveult et al., 2016.

claim: BRG1 is essential for maintaining ESC pluripotency.
source: BRG1, like OCT4, is essential for maintaining ESC pluripotency (Ho et al., 2009; Kidder et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014), supporting early embryonic development (Bultman et al., 2006) and improving the efficiency of iPSC reprogramming (Singhal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2009; Kidder et al., 2009; and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: BRG1 supports early embryonic development.
source: BRG1, like OCT4, is essential for maintaining ESC pluripotency (Ho et al., 2009; Kidder et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014), supporting early embryonic development (Bultman et al., 2006) and improving the efficiency of iPSC reprogramming (Singhal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bultman et al., 2006.

claim: BRG1 improves the efficiency of iPSC reprogramming.
source: BRG1, like OCT4, is essential for maintaining ESC pluripotency (Ho et al., 2009; Kidder et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014), supporting early embryonic development (Bultman et al., 2006) and improving the efficiency of iPSC reprogramming (Singhal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singhal et al., 2010.

claim: Chromatin accessibility was reduced at the majority of OCT4-bound sites following BRG1 depletion.
source: When we extended this analysis to all OCT4-bound sites, it was clear that chromatin accessibility was reduced (Figure 3I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and nucleosome occupancy increased following BRG1 depletion at the majority of OCT4 target sites (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nucleosome occupancy increased following BRG1 depletion at the majority of OCT4 target sites.
source: When we extended this analysis to all OCT4-bound sites, it was clear that chromatin accessibility was reduced (Figure 3I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and nucleosome occupancy increased following BRG1 depletion at the majority of OCT4 target sites (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by nucleosome occupancy data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 45% of OCT4-bound sites showed significantly reduced ATAC-seq signal following BRG1 removal using a stringent threshold (fold change >1.5 and FDR < 0.05).
source: We then used a stringent threshold (fold change >1.5 and FDR < 0.05) to identify sites that experienced significant reductions in chromatin accessibility following BRG1 removal. This revealed that 45% of OCT4-bound sites showed significantly reduced ATAC-seq signal and these sites were also highly dependent on OCT4 for their accessibility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by differential binding analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 76% of OCT4-bound sites that rely on OCT4 for their accessibility were also dependent on BRG1 for their accessibility.
source: Indeed, when we applied an unbiased clustering approach to examine the relationship between removal of OCT4 and BRG1 in shaping accessibility it was clear that the majority (76%) of OCT4-bound sites that rely on OCT4 for their accessibility were also dependent on BRG1 for their accessibility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Loss of either OCT4 or BRG1 resulted in similar reductions in chromatin accessibility across nearly all OCT4 peaks.
source: Importantly, the loss of either OCT4 or BRG1 appeared to result in similar, although not identical, reductions in chromatin accessibility across nearly all OCT4 peaks (Figure 3I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), revealing that both of these factors are required to maintain chromatin accessibility at these loci in mouse ESCs.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of ATAC-seq changes shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Large scale proteomic studies have indicated that BRG1 may interact physically with OCT4.
source: Given that large scale proteomic studies have previously indicated that BRG1 may interact physically with OCT4 (Pardo et al., 2010; van den Berg et al., 2010; Ding et al., 2012), and BRG1 is enriched at OCT4-bound sites throughout the genome (Figure 3), we favoured the possibility that OCT4 recruits BRG1 and the associated BAF complex to OCT4 target sites in the genome in order to remodel chromatin and promote chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pardo et al., 2010; van den Berg et al., 2010; and Ding et al., 2012.

claim: OCT4, BRG1 and SS18 are enriched within the nucleosome-depleted region at OCT4 target sites.
source: In fitting with this possibility, OCT4, BRG1 and the additional BAF subunit, SS18, are enriched within the nucleosome-depleted region at OCT4 target sites (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by high-resolution metaplot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A dramatic reduction in BRG1 and SS18 binding at OCT4 target sites was observed in the absence of OCT4.
source: Although BRG1 and SS18 protein levels were unaffected following removal of OCT4 (Figure 1A), we observed a dramatic reduction in BRG1 and SS18 binding at OCT4 target sites in the absence of OCT4 (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data for BRG1 and SS18 shown in Figure 4B,C and protein levels shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Loss of BRG1 and SS18 at OCT4 binding sites was specific to OCT4-bound regulatory elements as regulatory elements lacking OCT4 were unaffected.
source: This loss was specific to OCT4-bound regulatory elements as regulatory elements lacking OCT4 were unaffected (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4D comparing OCT4-bound and OCT4-free sites.

claim: There was a good correlation between the loss of BRG1 and SS18 and loss of ATAC-seq signal at OCT4 binding sites in OCT4-depleted ESCs.
source: Indeed, when we compared reductions in chromatin accessibility with reductions in BRG1 and SS18 at OCT4 binding sites, there was a good correlation between the loss of these factors and loss of ATAC-seq signal in OCT4-depleted ESCs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: BRG1 is recruited to pluripotency-associated enhancers coincident with the formation of accessible chromatin during iPSC reprogramming.
source: Interestingly, our observation that OCT4 recruits the BRG1/BAF complex to its target sites in ESCs is in agreement with recent observations that BRG1 is recruited to pluripotency-associated enhancers coincident with the formation of accessible chromatin during iPSC reprogramming (Chronis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chronis et al., 2017.

claim: 60% of distal OCT4 targets showed significant reductions in OCT4 binding following BRG1 removal (FDR < 0.05 and fold change >1.5 fold).
source: Strikingly, we observed significant reductions in OCT4 binding at the majority (60%; FDR < 0.05 and fold change >1.5 fold) of distal OCT4 targets following BRG1 removal (Figure 5A–C), indicating that BRG1 contributes not only to creating accessibility at OCT4 target sites but is also required to sustain normal OCT4 binding in mouse ESCs.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: SOX2 and NANOG binding was significantly reduced following BRG1 removal in ESCs (16.7% and 22.9% of distal OCT4 target sites; FDR < 0.05 and fold change >1.5 fold).
source: Similarly, SOX2 and NANOG binding was also significantly reduced following BRG1 removal in ESCs, although the total number of sites significantly affected was less than for OCT4 (16.7% and 22.9% of distal OCT4 target sites; FDR < 0.05 and fold change >1.5 fold) (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Loss of BRG1 did not result in complete loss of transcription factor binding at the most extremely affected OCT4 target sites, yet resulted in an inability of the cells to maintain the nucleosome-depleted state.
source: Importantly, even when we examined the most extremely affected OCT4 target sites (BRG1-dependent), loss of BRG1 did not result in complete loss of transcription factor binding (Figure 5D), yet resulted in an inability of the cells to maintain the nucleosome-depleted state (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 5D and nucleosome occupancy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression of genes associated with sites that rely on BRG1 for OCT4 binding tended to be reduced following deletion of BRG1.
source: Importantly, this analysis revealed that the expression of genes associated with sites that rely on BRG1 for OCT4 binding tended to be reduced following deletion of BRG1 (Figure 5E–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E-G and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Genes associated with unchanged or increased OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG binding tended to show increases in expression following BRG1 removal.
source: In contrast, genes associated with unchanged or increased OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG binding tended to show increases in expression (Figure 5E–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E-G and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Distal OCT4 binding sites in close proximity to OCT4/BRG1 dependent genes experienced the largest reductions in transcription factor binding following removal of BRG1.
source: Furthermore, distal OCT4 binding sites in close proximity to OCT4/BRG1 dependent genes experienced the largest reductions in transcription factor binding following removal of BRG1 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Genes associated with BRG1-independent OCT4 binding were activated early during reprogramming and BRG1-dependent sites later.
source: This revealed that genes associated with BRG1-independent OCT4 binding were activated early during reprogramming and BRG1-dependent sites later (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of reprogramming time course data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Genes that require BRG1 for OCT4 binding were expressed later during reprogramming.
source: In contrast, genes that require BRG1 for OCT4 binding were expressed later during reprogramming, perhaps because OCT4 requires BRG1 at these sites to remodel chromatin and mature the function of these regulatory elements.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of reprogramming time course data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: BRG1-dependent OCT4 binding sites were associated with genes expressed at later developmental stages during early mouse development.
source: In fitting with this possibility, BRG1-dependent OCT4 binding sites were also associated with genes expressed at later developmental stages during early mouse development (Figure 6B), suggesting that chromatin state in the early embryo may also shape how these OCT4 target sites are used during development.
evidence: This is supported by GREAT annotation analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: BRG1-dependent OCT4 target sites became accessible at later stages of embryonic development.
source: Interestingly, this demonstrated that BRG1-dependent OCT4 target sites became accessible at later stages of embryonic development (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq and DNase-seq data during early development shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: OCT4 occupies sites that would otherwise be inaccessible and is required to shape the occupancy of additional pluripotency transcription factors.
source: In doing so we discover that OCT4 occupies sites that would otherwise be inaccessible and is required to shape the occupancy of additional pluripotency transcription factors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: OCT4 achieves shaping of transcription factor occupancy by recruiting the chromatin remodelling factor BRG1 to support not only its own binding but also to stabilize further transcription factor binding events required to support pluripotency-associated gene regulation.
source: OCT4 achieves this by recruiting the chromatin remodelling factor BRG1 to support not only its own binding but also to stabilize further transcription factor binding events required to support pluripotency-associated gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 3-5.

claim: The pioneering activities of OCT4 are required not only during reprogramming, but also in the established pluripotent state.
source: This suggests that the pioneering activities of OCT4 are required not only during reprogramming, but also in the established pluripotent state.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on findings from Figures 1 and 2.

claim: OCT4 may be able to dynamically sample its target sites throughout the genome through its capacity to bind nucleosomal DNA.
source: A requirement of this process is OCT4's ability to engage with sequences in inaccessible chromatin presumably through its capacity to bind nucleosomal DNA (Figure 1; Soufi et al., 2012, 2015), suggesting that OCT4 may be able to dynamically sample its target sites throughout the genome.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 1 and citations to Soufi et al., 2012, 2015.

claim: Cooperation with BRG1 is required for more stable OCT4 binding.
source: However, cooperation with BRG1 appears to be required for more stable OCT4 binding (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Enhanced OCT4 binding was observed during OCT4-SOX2-KLF4 reprogramming when BRG1 was included in the reprogramming cocktail.
source: This general model is consistent with previous experiments that showed enhanced OCT4 binding during OCT4-SOX2-KLF4 reprogramming when BRG1 was included in the reprogramming cocktail (Singhal et al., 2010) and is in agreement with our observation that BRG1 is required for normal chromatin accessibility and OCT4 binding at otherwise inaccessible and inactive regulatory elements.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singhal et al., 2010.

claim: When ESCs are transitioned into epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs), OCT4 stably associates with a new set of previously inaccessible sites in a manner that appears to rely on co-binding of the EpiLC-specific transcription factor OTX2.
source: In fitting with this possibility, when ESCs are transitioned into epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs), OCT4 stably associates with a new set of previously inaccessible sites in a manner that appears to rely on co-binding of the EpiLC-specific transcription factor OTX2 (Buecker et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Buecker et al., 2014 and Yang et al., 2014.

claim: OCT4 is the only Yamanaka transcription factor that cannot be substituted for in iPSC reprogramming experiments.
source: In agreement with these general ideas, OCT4 appears to be the only Yamanaka transcription factor that cannot be substituted for in iPSC reprogramming experiments, suggesting its pioneering activity is fundamental in establishing and maintaining the pluripotency network in concert with SOX2, KLF4 and c-Myc (Nakagawa et al., 2008; Sterneckert et al., 2012), perhaps due to its cooperation with BRG1 (Singhal et al., 2010; Esch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakagawa et al., 2008; Sterneckert et al., 2012; Singhal et al., 2010; and Esch et al., 2013.

claim: FoxA1 can stably bind its target sites and directly alter nucleosomal structure through steric disruption of histone:DNA contacts.
source: While some pioneer factors, such as FoxA1, can stably bind their target sites and directly alter nucleosomal structure through steric disruption of histone:DNA contacts (Cirillo et al., 2002; Hatta and Cirillo, 2007; Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016), the extent to which other pioneer factors might exploit such a mechanism has yet to be fully addressed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cirillo et al., 2002; Hatta and Cirillo, 2007; and Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016.

claim: OCT4 does not have an intrinsic chromatin opening activity, but requires cooperation with BRG1 to achieve this.
source: In the case of OCT4, our observations establish that its capacity to support transcription factor binding and chromatin accessibility requires the chromatin remodeller BRG1. This suggests that unlike FoxA1, OCT4 does not have an intrinsic chromatin opening activity, but requires cooperation with BRG1 to achieve this.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on findings from Figures 3-5.

claim: The pioneer factor GATA3 has similar dependency on BRG1 in creating accessible chromatin.
source: Indeed, our work on OCT4 is generally consistent with and supported by recent work studying the pioneer factor GATA3 which appears to have similar dependency on BRG1 in creating accessible chromatin (Takaku et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takaku et al., 2016.

claim: Chromatin remodelling activity has been widely implicated in shaping nucleosome positioning and chromatin accessibility at target sites bound by other pioneer transcription factors.
source: Furthermore, chromatin remodelling activity has been widely implicated in shaping nucleosome positioning and chromatin accessibility at target sites bound by other pioneer transcription factors (Hu et al., 2011; Sanalkumar et al., 2014; Ceballos-Chávez et al., 2015; Hainer and Fazzio, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2011; Sanalkumar et al., 2014; Ceballos-Chávez et al., 2015; and Hainer and Fazzio, 2015.
